description: One of Oudolf Garden Detroit's signature plants. 'Fatal Attraction' is a compact selection with intense rosy-purple petals surrounding nearly black centers. It blooms prolifically through summer and the spiny seed heads persist as bird food through winter. Found throughout the A Beds.
waterRequirement: Low to medium; drought-tolerant once established
distinguishingFeatures: Reflexed (drooping) rosy-purple petals surrounding a spiny orange-brown dome — the cone shape is diagnostic
Compact mounded form with nearly black stems and buds — very dark for a coneflower cultivar
Rough, sandpaper-like leaves and stiff hairy stems
Seed heads persist all winter, turning dark as goldfinches methodically extract seeds

description: Tall magenta-purple spikes that bloom from top to bottom — the opposite of most flower spikes. A monarch butterfly magnet during fall migration. Native to tallgrass prairies of the Midwest, it is a vertical punctuation in the A Beds throughout July and August.
waterRequirement: Medium; tolerates occasional flooding and drought
distinguishingFeatures: Flowers open sequentially from TOP of spike downward — opposite of most flowering plants
Dense, fluffy magenta-purple button-like blooms packed tightly on an upright spike
Grass-like narrow leaves clasp the stem all the way up
Perfectly vertical, exclamation-mark shape — a strong visual accent among surrounding plants

description: Perennial Plant of the Year 2011. Prized for two seasons: pale blue star-shaped flowers in spring, and extraordinary feathery foliage turning brilliant golden-orange in fall. Appears throughout the A, B, and C Beds, providing long-season structure and interest.
nativeRange: Arkansas and Oklahoma (narrowly endemic to the Ouachita Mountains)
waterRequirement: Low to medium; drought-tolerant once established
distinguishingFeatures: Feathery needle-like foliage (not typical broad leaf) forms a soft, perfectly arching mound
Clusters of tiny pale blue star-shaped flowers in spring — subtle but beautiful close up
Fall foliage turns brilliant golden-orange, among the best fall color of any garden perennial
Milky sap if stems are broken — characteristic of the Apocynaceae (dogbane) family

description: Brilliant orange flower clusters on a native milkweed. Critical host plant for monarch butterfly caterpillars — monarchs can only reproduce on milkweed. Unlike most milkweeds, butterfly weed does not produce milky latex sap. Found in the A Beds.
waterRequirement: Low; excellent drainage required — very drought-tolerant
distinguishingFeatures: Clusters of brilliant orange (occasionally yellow-orange) flowers — no other native milkweed has this color
Clear (not milky) sap when stem is broken — differs from most milkweed species
Slow to emerge in spring — mark the location to avoid digging it accidentally
Long narrow seed pods split open in fall to release silky-parachuted seeds

description: A Piet Oudolf signature plant — 'Hummelo' was named after Oudolf's own garden in the Netherlands. Dense, compact spikes of rosy-violet flowers bloom for weeks without deadheading. Its neat mounded form and long bloom season make it a cornerstone of the A and B Beds.
nativeRange: Europe (widely used in naturalistic planting design)
distinguishingFeatures: Dense cylindrical flower spikes packed with tiny purple-violet blooms
Upright, tidy habit — does not sprawl or need staking even in wind
Basal leaves are deeply wrinkled (rugose) and hairy with a pleasant minty-herbal scent
Blooms nearly non-stop for 6–8 weeks — far longer than most salvias or veronicas

description: Intense violet-purple flat-topped flower clusters in late summer make ironweed one of the most vivid plants in the A and B Beds. The name refers to the incredibly tough, wiry stems. A magnet for monarchs and swallowtails during fall migration.
distinguishingFeatures: Intense violet-purple flat-topped corymbs — one of the most saturated purples in the autumn garden
Stems are wiry and rigid — nearly impossible to bend, hence 'ironweed'
Fluffy silver-white seed heads persist after bloom, catching morning light beautifully
Very tall — creates bold vertical accents among fall grasses and seed heads

description: One of the last plants to bloom in the garden — 'October Skies' covers itself with sky-blue daisy-like flowers in late September and October, just as most other plants wind down. The foliage is fragrant when crushed. A critical late-season nectar source for migrating monarchs.
distinguishingFeatures: Masses of small lavender-blue daisy flowers in October when almost nothing else blooms
Foliage has a pleasant aromatic scent when rubbed — like a wild herb
Compact mounded habit; stays tidy without staking even in wind
Critical late-season nectar source for migrating monarchs and late-flying native bees

description: One of the most distinctive plants in the A Beds — spiky yucca-like leaves and spherical silver-white flower heads on rigid blue-green stems. Despite its menacing appearance, it is beloved by native bees. Native Americans used the roots medicinally; the common name reflects this historical use.
distinguishingFeatures: Long strap-like bluish-green leaves edged with small spines — looks remarkably like a yucca
Spherical golf-ball-sized white flower heads on rigid branching stems
Blue-green waxy stem color — very distinctive against surrounding green foliage
Seed heads dry silver-white and persist through winter as structural accents

description: Despite its common name (which comes from using dried leaves as snuff, not from allergies), this is a spectacular late-summer plant. 'Sahin's Early Flowerer' produces hundreds of golden-yellow to russet-red daisies from July onward — one of the earliest and longest-blooming heleniums.
distinguishingFeatures: Daisy flowers with reflexed (downward-curving) petals angling back from a prominent central cone
Color ranges from golden-yellow to russet-red and bicolor — often different hues on the same plant
Heavily branched, creating a cloud of blooms from midsummer through fall
Central cone is prominent and velvety — deeper brown/red than surrounding petals

description: The iconic grass of the tallgrass prairie — once covering over 140 million acres of the American Midwest. 'Dancing Wind' moves beautifully in the breeze. Turns copper-red to maroon in fall and winter, providing structural interest in the A Beds for months after the forbs have faded.
nativeRange: Central and Eastern North America (tallgrass prairie)
waterRequirement: Low to medium; drought-tolerant with very deep roots
distinguishingFeatures: Distinctive three-pronged seed head resembles a turkey foot — the vernacular 'turkeyfoot grass'
Turns vivid copper-red to burgundy-maroon in fall; holds color through winter
Blue-green foliage in summer — bluer than most native grasses
Very deep roots (up to 12 feet) help it reach groundwater during drought

description: A hybrid baptisia with deep navy-blue flowers in spring — among the most striking blues in the B Beds. Grows into a large, shrub-like clump over years. The rattling inflated seed pods turn black in late summer. As a legume, it fixes nitrogen in the soil.
waterRequirement: Low to medium; drought-tolerant once established
distinguishingFeatures: Intensely deep navy-blue pea-shaped flowers — among the darkest blues in the spring garden
Inflated seed pods turn jet black and rattle when shaken in late summer (like baby rattles)
Blue-green glaucous foliage persists as a handsome shrub-like form all season
Extremely slow-growing but exceptionally long-lived — established clumps can be decades old

description: Also known as 'May Night' sage, this is one of the most floriferous plants in the B Beds. Dense spikes of deep indigo-violet flowers appear in late spring with strong rebloom if cut back. A foundational plant in Oudolf's palette for its clarity of color and compact, reliable form.
distinguishingFeatures: Very deep indigo-violet flower spikes — nearly black-purple at bud stage
Aromatic leaves with a pleasant sage scent when brushed
Red-purple calyces (flower cups) persist after petals drop, extending the ornamental season
Reblooms reliably if cut back hard after first flush — can continue May through August

description: 'Firetail' is one of the longest-blooming plants in the garden — slender crimson-red bottlebrush spikes appear from July and continue until hard frost. Used in both the A and B Beds. The clasping leaves are distinctive and the plant forms a dense, slowly spreading clump.
distinguishingFeatures: Slender crimson-red bottlebrush spikes, narrower and more fiery than other persicaria cultivars
Blooms July until frost — among the longest bloom seasons of any garden perennial
Large heart-shaped leaves clasp the stem at their base (amplexicaulis = stem-clasping)
Spreads slowly by rhizomes into a dense clump; does not self-seed aggressively

description: The silvery-white bracts surrounding the small flowers create a luminous frosted effect from midsummer through fall. One of the most important native pollinator plants — on warm days it can be covered with dozens of native bee species simultaneously. Key in both the A and B Beds.
distinguishingFeatures: Silver-white bracts (modified leaves) around the flowers glow like silver buttons from July through fall
Strong mint scent when foliage is crushed — pleasant and cooling on a hot day
Often covered with more bee species simultaneously than almost any other garden plant
Spreads by stolons into a colony — can be more vigorous in rich moist soils

description: The primary matrix grass of the B Beds. Fine-textured arching mounds of emerald foliage with a remarkable fragrance — the seed heads smell of buttered popcorn or cilantro in late summer. Turns golden-orange in fall and holds its graceful form through winter.
distinguishingFeatures: Extremely fine, hair-like foliage forms a perfect cascading fountain shape
Seed heads have a surprising buttered-popcorn or cilantro fragrance — lean in close!
Turns warm golden-orange in fall and holds through winter without flopping
Slow to establish but very long-lived; a mature clump may be many decades old

description: The earliest-blooming native monarda — pale lavender flowers with spotted lower petals in late spring, weeks before the better-known M. didyma. Highly resistant to powdery mildew. Found in the A, B, and C Beds, providing spring interest when few other plants are in bloom.
distinguishingFeatures: Pale lavender to white flowers with distinctive purple-spotted lower lip — subtle but beautiful close up
Blooms May–June, weeks earlier than most beebalms (Monarda didyma, M. fistulosa)
Square stems — characteristic of the entire mint family (Lamiaceae)
Strongly aromatic foliage with a wild oregano-thyme scent when crushed

description: A compact native rudbeckia with masses of golden-yellow daisy flowers with dark centers, blooming from August into October. 'Little Henry' is smaller and more compact than the species. The foliage has a pleasant anise-like fragrance. A key plant in the C Beds organic grouping scheme.
distinguishingFeatures: Golden-yellow petals surrounding a prominent dark brown to black central cone
Leaves and stems have soft gray-white hairs (subtomentosa = slightly woolly)
Foliage has a sweet anise fragrance when crushed — distinctive among black-eyed susans
Later-blooming and more compact than common Rudbeckia fulgida 'Goldsturm'

description: Perhaps the most widely planted perennial geranium in the world. 'Rozanne' produces violet-blue saucer-shaped flowers from late spring through frost with almost no interruption. It weaves between other plants in the C Beds, filling gaps and softening edges with its sprawling habit.
distinguishingFeatures: Violet-blue flowers with white centers and purple veining — cool blue rarely matched in summer
Blooms from May through hard frost — essentially a 6-month flowering season
Sprawling habit weaves between adjacent plants, filling gaps gracefully
Deeply cut palmate leaves turn red in fall for secondary seasonal interest

description: One of the most elegant irises for naturalistic planting — slender upright foliage and deep violet-blue flowers in late spring, followed by attractive seed pods that provide winter structure. Unlike bearded irises, highly adaptable and disease-resistant. Featured in both the B and C Beds.
distinguishingFeatures: Deep violet-blue flowers with yellow signal marks on the falls — richly saturated color
Narrow, upright grass-like foliage persists and turns golden-tan in fall
Distinctive rectangular seed capsules split open when ripe; valued as dried flower
Foliage remains attractive all season after bloom — unlike bearded iris which look untidy

description: A foundational grass throughout the A, B, and C Beds. 'Ha Ha Tonka' is compact and upright with blue-green summer foliage that transforms to brilliant copper-orange in fall. The fluffy silver-white seed heads glow in low-angle autumn sunlight. A signature of the American prairie.
distinguishingFeatures: Blue-green foliage in summer shifts to brilliant copper-orange to scarlet in fall
Fluffy silver-white seed heads catch late afternoon and early morning light magnificently
Upright, non-flopping habit — stays tidy and architectural even in winter
Blue summer color is due to a waxy surface coating; rub a leaf to feel the smooth texture

description: The most intensely red native wildflower in North America. The scarlet color is specifically evolved to attract hummingbirds, the primary pollinator — bees cannot see red as a color. Found in the Rain Garden, where it thrives in the consistently moist conditions along the stormwater channels.
waterRequirement: Medium to moist; thrives near water
distinguishingFeatures: Intense scarlet-red tubular flowers — the most vivid red of any native North American perennial
Two-lipped flowers: three petals form a lower lip, two spread wide above — very distinctive shape
Hummingbirds hover briefly at each flower — watch from the path for visits
Self-seeds freely in moist areas; short-lived perennial that reliably self-perpetuates

description: A graceful spring native with pendant red-and-yellow flowers that nod gently on slender stems. The distinctive backward-pointing spurs are filled with nectar accessible to hummingbirds and long-tongued bumblebees. Found in the Rain Garden, blooming in April–May before summer plants take over.
waterRequirement: Low to medium; tolerates dry shade
distinguishingFeatures: Five red petals forming backward-pointing hollow spurs filled with nectar — an unmistakable nodding lantern shape
Yellow stamens and inner petals contrast brilliantly with the outer red spurs
Delicate blue-green compound leaves remain attractive long after bloom ends
Self-seeds readily in moist, shaded spots — look for seedlings throughout the rain garden

description: A tall, stately native lobelia with brilliant blue flower spikes in late summer. Found in both the A Beds and the Rain Garden. Planted next to cardinal flower, the blue-and-red combination is spectacular. A crucial late-season nectar source for bumblebees, which are its primary pollinators.
waterRequirement: Medium to moist; tolerates wet feet
distinguishingFeatures: Brilliant medium-blue flower spikes — blue is rare and unusual in late-summer native wildflowers
Flowers have a distinctive white stripe on the lower lip — a close look reveals the detail
Grows naturally along stream edges; more tolerant of wet feet than most perennials
Spectacular planted near red cardinal flower — blue and red complement each other perfectly

description: A native Louisiana iris with unusual copper to brick-red flowers — among the few truly orange-toned native irises in North America. Found in the Rain Garden, where it naturalizes along the water's edge in moist soil. The flat, strap-like leaves are distinctive among irises.
waterRequirement: Moist to wet; thrives in standing water
distinguishingFeatures: Copper, brick-red to orange-red flowers — unusual warm tone very different from typical purple irises
Pendant falls (lower petals) droop downward, lacking the typical upright standards of bearded iris
Flat, strap-like flexible leaves grow in fans — more pliable than the stiff Siberian iris
Spreads by rhizomes into dense colonies in wet soils along the rain garden edge
